newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bolger sees lower rates, stable NZD if re-elected.
newsitem.headline: Bolger sees lower rates, stable NZD if re-elected.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Monday interest rates would start to come off in the new year, inflation pressures would ease and the currency would stabilise if the conservative National government was re-elected.
Speaking to a Wellington Chamber of Commerce luncheon, Bolger said growth would rebound from its current trough of 2.1 percent to around 3.5 percent to four percent.
He said his view was based on the assumptions in Treasury's pre-election fiscal and economic update, released in September.
"We will go back up to 3.5 percent to four percent growth and sustain that in general terms through the expansion of industry.

"Interest rates would come down in the new year if our programme is in place. I don't think there is any doubt about that. They have started to ease off at the present moment and they would continue to come down in the new year," Bolger said.

"We will see the peak come off the inflation pressure -- that is coming off now. And we would anticipate that the dollar will stabilise rather than that long, strong surge up that it has been. Not stabilise for ever, but stabilise where it has been growing very, very strongly."
He said by contrast a Labour-led government would see a lot more spending, higher interest rates, rising inflationary concerns and more trade union power.
"Progressively we would slow down from going forward and gently start to glide back."
Asked if the National Party had missed the boat by not making sufficient deals with potential coalition partners, Bolger said it had not, but there was a possibility of further deals in future years.
National is averaging 35 percent in the polls and its potential coalition partners are struggling to make the five percent level at which they are assured of seats after the October 12 election.
The three main opposition parties -- Labour, economic nationalist New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance -- are together attracting around 52 percent support on average.
Bolger outlined various "freedoms" his government stood for in a speech which was more positive than his party's recent campaign warning of a "crash of 1997" if National is not re-elected.

They included freedom from excessive tax, high mortgage rates and debt and the freedom to have a job without union control, to have a welfare safety net and the freedom to resolve Maori land claims in a fair and affordable way.
